# NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA): investment memo

**Recommendation: Avoid for now. Size today: 0% of the portfolio. Planned: 3.7% if the 17 November report passes two tests, then 7.4% after the February annual report.**

From the analyst to the portfolio manager. Written 2026-09-23 from prices and filings as of the close on 2026-09-22.

An investment memo is the note in which an analyst asks the portfolio manager (PM), the person who decides what the portfolio owns and in what size, to act. The action is one of seven. Initiate is buying a first holding, Add is buying more, Hold is keeping it, Trim is selling part and Exit is selling all. Avoid is owning none, and Short is selling borrowed shares, a trade that profits if the price falls. My Avoid is not a forecast that the shares will fall. Position size is a holding's value as a share of the portfolio's value. NVIDIA's fiscal year, the twelve months its accounts cover, ends in late January, so fiscal 2027 (FY2027) is the year to January 2027.

**Expected return and bear loss.** The bull, base and bear cases are the good, middle and bad outcomes I think plausible, each built from stated assumptions. Gross margin is revenue minus the cost of revenue (the cost of the goods sold), as a share of revenue. The probability-weighted value multiplies each case's value by its probability and adds the results. The expected return is that value's percentage gain on the last close. The required return is the annual return a stock must offer to pay for its risk, and for NVIDIA I put it at 12.0% (section 7).

| Case | Probability | Value in 12 months | Return from $228.87 | What has to happen |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 25% | $370 | +61.7% | Revenue grows 43% in FY2028 and 21% in FY2029, with gross margin near 74% |
| Base | 50% | $260 | +13.6% | Revenue grows 30% in FY2028 and 12% in FY2029, with gross margin easing to 72% |
| Bear | 25% | $125 | -45.4% | Growth slows to 5% in FY2028, then revenue falls 24% and gross margin 8 points in FY2029, a repeat of FY2023 |
| Probability-weighted | | $253.75 | +10.9%; +11.3% with $1.00 of dividends | |
| Required return | | | +12.0% | |

The price target, my estimate of what the shares will be worth in 12 months and the figure my record is scored against, is $255. It is the weighted value rounded to the nearest $5, 11.4% above the last close.

**Why this size.** Volatility measures how widely a stock's daily price changes vary, stated as a yearly figure. NVIDIA's was 37.8% over the past year. The portfolio's sizing rule sets each holding's risk budget, its size times its volatility, at 2.8%, which gives NVIDIA a full size of 7.4%. I recommend 0% today. A percentage point is the unit of difference between two percentages. The expected total return of 11.3% is 0.7 percentage points below the 12.0% required, so a holding would add risk and no expected reward. One outcome in four loses 45%. If the November report passes both tests, the expected return rises to about 24% (section 2). I would then buy half the full size, 3.7%, so that the bear case costs the portfolio 1.7% rather than 3.4%. I would move to 7.4% when the annual report shows the cash catching up with the profit.

**Thesis.** An investment thesis is the short argument for why a stock is mispriced, or why it is not. NVIDIA's next year of earnings is well supported, but $228.87 already pays for my base case, so I would wait for two reports before buying.

**Why now.** The reports that settle the open questions are due within five months: the October-quarter report on 17 November, 55 days away, and the annual report in late February. Setting the rules for buying and selling now means the decision rests on the tests, not on how the price reacts to each report.

**The three things that matter most.**

1. *Growth into FY2028.* Guidance, management's own published forecast, calls for October-quarter revenue of $108.0 billion, up 12.2% on July. My base case needs FY2028 Data Center growth of 32%, and the price needs about 30% (section 1). The first test is January-quarter guidance of $125 billion or more. Guidance below $108.0 billion, a fall from October, would move me toward the bear case.
2. *Profit turning into cash.* GAAP results follow US accounting rules, and non-GAAP results are the company's adjusted version, which leaves out items it considers unusual. Cash conversion, the share of profit that arrives as cash from operations, fell from 86% of GAAP profit in FY2026. In the first half of FY2027 it was 75% of non-GAAP profit. Accounts receivable, the money customers owe for goods already delivered, grew faster than sales. Days sales outstanding (DSO), receivables divided by a quarter's revenue times 91 days, rose from 51 to 60. The second test is DSO at or below 55 days in October. On guided revenue that caps receivables at $65.3 billion, against $63.1 billion in July.
3. *Customer financing.* Three direct customers provided 44% of first-half revenue. NVIDIA also holds $99 billion of equity investments and has $36 billion of cloud service commitments to AI cloud partners. It has guaranteed up to $105 billion of payments on a campus leased to OpenAI. If those customers find it harder to raise money, orders could fall faster than the use of artificial intelligence.

## 1. What is priced in

What is priced in means the growth and margins that today's price needs in order to be a fair price. A valuation multiple is a price divided by a measure of profit or size, such as P/E. I work back from the price over two spans: the next 12 months, from the multiple, and the next ten years, from cash flows.

**The next 12 months.** To earn the 12% required return, the shares must be worth $255.33 in September 2027, after $1.00 of dividends. Next twelve months (NTM) means the four quarters following a given date. Today NVIDIA trades at 20.8 times my estimate of its NTM EPS, $11.03. If buyers still pay 21 times in September 2027, $255.33 needs NTM EPS of $12.16 at that date. My base case gives $12.34. Holding my other assumptions, $12.16 needs FY2028 Data Center revenue to grow 30.2%.

**The next ten years.** A discounted cash flow (DCF) model values a company as the sum of its future free cash flows, each reduced to today's money. The discount rate is the annual return an investor requires for the risk, used to make that reduction. A reverse DCF works backwards from the price to the growth it requires. Holding my forecasts to FY2029 and discounting at 12%, the price needs free cash flow to grow 22.0% a year from FY2030 to FY2034, and 3% a year after that. My base case fades growth from 10% to 3% over those five years.

The free cash flow margin is free cash flow as a share of revenue, and mine is 43.3% in FY2029. At that margin, the $690.5 billion of free cash flow that the price needs in FY2034 would take revenue of about $1,594 billion. That is 2.13 times the $747 billion that the 41 listed companies in the Semiconductors sub-industry with stored figures reported together over the past 12 months.

Higher margins alone cannot close the gap. On my growth path, cash flow from FY2030 would need to be 1.82 times my base case, a free cash flow margin of 78.7%. Net margin is net income as a share of revenue, and mine is 51.4% for FY2029. In my model free cash flow is a share of net income, never more than all of it, so the gap has to come from growth.

| Measure | The price requires | My base case |
|---|---|---|
| NTM EPS in September 2027, at 21 times | $12.16 | $12.34 |
| FY2028 Data Center revenue growth | 30.2% | 32% |
| FY2028 total revenue growth | 28.8% | 30% |
| Free cash flow growth a year, FY2030 to FY2034, at a 12% discount rate | 22.0% | 10% fading to 3% |
| The same at an 11% or 10% discount rate | 18.1% or 14.1% | 10% fading to 3% |
| Free cash flow in FY2034 | $690.5 billion | $346.5 billion |
| Value today if growth is 3% a year after FY2029 | | $120 a share |

The two spans agree once the multiple is accounted for. The 12-month figure assumes that buyers in September 2027 still pay 21 times earnings, and the ten-year figure shows what that multiple requires. The price matches my base case for the next year and needs far more than it after FY2029.

Against other chip companies (section 4), NVIDIA's P/E of 28.9 is below the median of 46.3 for seven peers. It has fallen 43% in a year, because EPS rose 125% while the price rose 29%.

## 2. Where I disagree

Variant perception is where my forecast differs from what the price requires, together with a checkable reason the price has not yet moved. On the next 12 months I have none. The price requires FY2028 Data Center growth of 30.2% and I forecast 32%. My expected total return is 0.7 points below the required return, a gap inside the error of my own inputs. With a beta of 1.46 instead of my 1.61, the two would be equal. I also cannot say whether my figures sit above or below other analysts' forecasts.

After FY2029 I have no evidence either way. My DCF value is below the price in every case, but I cannot test that within 12 months, so I do not base the recommendation on it.

**Where a variant view could come from.** The January-quarter guidance is the one number due soon that could separate my view from the price. At $125 billion, 15.7% above October, it would exceed the 12% rise in my bull case. Rerunning all three cases with that one figure changed gives values of $375, $265 and $130. With the same probabilities the expected total return would be 13.5%, only 1.5 points above the required return. I would also move 10 points of probability from the bear case to the bull case, because a quarter that strong makes a stall in FY2028 less likely. That step is my judgment. With probabilities of 35% bull, 50% base and 15% bear, the weighted value is $283.25 and the expected total return 24.2%. The price cannot already reflect that guidance, because it will not exist until 17 November.

## 3. The business

NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs), processors that run many calculations in parallel, and builds them into complete data center systems. These combine GPUs, central processors, networking chips, switches and software into racks that its 10-K says can join hundreds of thousands of GPUs into one computer. The 10-K is the annual report a US company files with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and the 10-Q is the quarterly version. Buyers use the systems for training, the process of building an artificial intelligence model from data, and for inference, running a trained model to produce answers. NVIDIA also sells GeForce graphics cards for gaming PCs, RTX workstation GPUs, and computers and software for self-driving cars and robots.

The company is fabless, meaning it designs its chips but pays outside foundries and contract manufacturers to make them. Its main costs are therefore the purchased chips, memory, boards and components in its cost of revenue, and the engineers and computing time behind its research.

**How it makes money.** NVIDIA's gross margin was 75.0% in the July quarter, against 72.4% a year earlier. Management attributes the rise to a better mix of Blackwell Ultra systems; Blackwell is the current platform and still the majority of shipments. Operating expenses are the costs of running the business beyond making the product, mainly research and development. They were $8.4 billion, or 8.8% of revenue, and rose 55% from a year earlier while revenue rose 106%. Operating income is the profit left after those expenses, and operating margin is operating income as a share of revenue; it was 66.2%.

Other income is income from outside operations, and NVIDIA says its own is mostly gains and losses on the shares it holds in other companies. It added $24.1 billion to first-half pre-tax profit, 17% of the total, and most of it was unrealised gains, increases in the value of holdings that have not been sold. That income can reverse. First-half EPS was $4.85 under GAAP and $4.09 non-GAAP, which excludes those equity gains and acquisition costs. I forecast on the non-GAAP basis because the equity gains cannot be forecast. Since the April 2026 quarter that basis includes stock-based compensation, the cost of paying employees in shares.

**Segments.** A segment is a part of the business for which the company reports revenue and profit separately. NVIDIA reports two.

| July 2026 quarter | Revenue | Share of revenue | Segment operating income | Segment operating margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Compute & Networking | $88.3 billion | 91.8% | $62.7 billion | 71.0% |
| Graphics | $7.9 billion | 8.2% | $3.9 billion | 49.2% |
| Total | $96.2 billion | 100% | $66.6 billion before unallocated costs | |

NVIDIA also splits revenue by market platform. Data Center was $89.0 billion (92.5% of revenue): $48.7 billion from Hyperscale, the very large cloud computing companies, and $40.3 billion from AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise. Edge Computing, which covers PCs, workstations, cars and robots, was $7.2 billion.

**Customers.** Direct customers are computer makers, contract manufacturers, cloud providers, AI model makers, system integrators and distributors. Many build systems for indirect customers such as AI clouds, enterprises and the public sector. Revenue concentration is the share of sales that comes from a few buyers. For the first half of FY2027, three direct customers were 16%, 15% and 13% of revenue. Management also estimates that one AI research company contributed "a meaningful amount" of revenue through NVIDIA's customers. By customer headquarters, the United States was 62.4% of July-quarter revenue, Taiwan 28.0% and China 8.2%.

## 4. Industry and peers

The 10-K's competition risk factor does not name rivals in the text stored for me. It says competitors' products "may be cheaper or provide better functionality", and that some competitors own their own chip factories. It also says some customers have "in-house expertise" to "develop their own solutions to replace those we are providing". Among the 41 listed companies in the Semiconductors sub-industry with stored figures, NVIDIA has 40.5% of combined revenue over the past 12 months. That is concentration among listed companies, not market share, which would need private and foreign rivals too.

**Peer comparison.** Comparable companies, or comps, are listed businesses similar enough that their valuation ratios give a reference point. I use the eight largest other companies in NVIDIA's sub-industry with stored 12-month figures, each over its latest reported 12 months. EV/revenue is enterprise value divided by revenue, useful when earnings are small or negative.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| Broadcom (AVGO) | 1,740 | 46.5 | 34.5 | 19.9 | 49% | 48% | 2.3% |

| Texas Instruments (TXN) | 248 | 41.2 | 27.2 | 13.1 | 17% | 37% | 2.2% |

n/m means not meaningful and n/a means not available; section 11 explains the gaps.

The table says three things. NVIDIA combines the second-fastest growth and the second-highest operating margin in the group with a P/E below five of the seven peers that have one. Micron, the one peer that grew faster at about the same margin, trades lower still, at 24.8 times earnings and 17.9 times EBITDA. That fits the archive's sector guide, which says a semiconductor P/E tends to be lowest at the peak of the cycle, when earnings are highest. On EV/EBITDA NVIDIA sits at the peer median, and its FCF yield is in line. NVIDIA is cheap against the group on earnings, but the group itself is not a guide to fair value (section 7).

A stock split gives each shareholder more shares, each worth proportionately less, and leaves the company's value unchanged. Filed EPS for early years uses the share count of the time. I restated it by dividing FY2015 to FY2019 by 40 and FY2020 to FY2022 by 10. Those factors are implied by the two jumps in the filed share count. Capital expenditure is spending on equipment and buildings, and the stored history has none, so there is no free cash flow column.

Two things changed. Until FY2023 NVIDIA was a smaller, cyclical business, meaning one whose profits rise and fall with its industry's spending rather than growing steadily. Its median operating margin from FY2015 to FY2023 was 27.2%. In FY2023 revenue was flat, gross margin fell 8.0 percentage points and operating income fell 58%. From FY2024 data center demand lifted revenue eightfold in three years and the operating margin to above 60%. Operating expenses took 39% of revenue in FY2015 and 11% in FY2026. Because the cost structure has changed, I do not value NVIDIA on its old average margin. Applied to the past year's revenue, that margin would give about $2.86 of EPS and a P/E of 80.

The published quarterly record shows an operating margin between 57.5% and 66.2% in eleven of the last twelve quarters. The exception is 49.1% in the April 2025 quarter, which carried a $4.5 billion charge for excess H20 inventory and purchase obligations.

The second change is in cash conversion. It fell from 94% in FY2024 to 86% in FY2026 and 75% of non-GAAP profit in the first half of FY2027.

## 7. Valuation

**Multiples.** I value NVIDIA on P/E because its earnings are large and positive. I apply it to NTM EPS as it will stand in September 2027, roughly half of FY2028 plus half of FY2029. A buyer then will be paying for the year ahead.

- Base, 21 times: today's NTM multiple held constant.
- Bull, 25 times: close to Micron's 24.8, the cheapest peer with comparable growth, and still far below the peer median of 46.3.
- Bear, 18 times: below every peer with positive earnings, because in this case NVIDIA's earnings are shrinking, while Qualcomm (22.6 times) has roughly flat revenue.

I do not apply the peer median directly. My base NTM EPS at 46.3 times would give $572, more than double the price. The median is set by companies with far lower margins or growth, and the whole group's prices rest on long-run assumptions of their own.

**Discounted cash flow.** The cost of equity is the required return for shareholders. The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) blends the cost of debt with the cost of equity by their weights in the company's capital. Debt is only 0.6% of NVIDIA's capital, so the WACC, the cost of equity and my discount rate are the same.

- *Cost of equity, 12%.* The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) sets the required return at the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium. The risk-free rate is the return on US government debt: 4.0%, from the stored 13-week Treasury bill. The Blume adjustment moves a measured beta one third of the way toward 1.0, because betas tend to drift there; it turns 1.91 into 1.61. The equity risk premium is the extra annual return required for owning shares instead of government debt, and 5% is my choice. The result is 4.0% + 1.61 x 5% = 12.0%.
- *Stages.* My model's free cash flow for the second half of FY2027 and for FY2028 and FY2029, then five years in which growth fades from 10% to 3%.
- *Terminal value, 3% growth.* A terminal value stands in for every year after the forecast, assuming cash flow grows at a constant rate forever. I use 3%, close to long-run growth in the US economy.
- *Timing.* The mid-year convention treats each year's cash as arriving in the middle of that year.

| Period | FCF ($B) | Years from today | Discount factor, 1/1.12^years | Present value ($B) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Second half FY2027 | 93.4 | 0.23 | 0.974 | 91.0 |
| FY2028 | 224.0 | 0.84 | 0.909 | 203.7 |
| FY2029 | 255.6 | 1.84 | 0.812 | 207.5 |
| FY2030 (+10%) | 281.2 | 2.84 | 0.725 | 203.8 |
| FY2031 (+8%) | 303.7 | 3.84 | 0.647 | 196.5 |
| FY2032 (+6%) | 321.9 | 4.84 | 0.578 | 186.0 |
| FY2033 (+4.5%) | 336.4 | 5.84 | 0.516 | 173.5 |
| FY2034 (+3%) | 346.5 | 6.84 | 0.461 | 159.6 |

Terminal value at FY2034 = 346.5 x 1.03 / (0.12 - 0.03) = $3,965 billion, worth $1,826 billion today. Equity value = $1,422 billion (the sum of the present values above) + $1,826 billion + $23.2 billion of net cash = $3,271 billion. Divided by 24.1 billion shares, that is $136 a share today. A year from now the value should have grown by the required return less the cash paid out: $136 x 1.12 less $1.00 of dividends gives $151.

| Discount rate | Terminal growth 2% | 3% | 4% |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10% | $159 | $174 | $194 |
| 11% | $142 | $152 | $166 |
| 12% | $127 | $136 | $146 |
| 13% | $116 | $122 | $130 |
| 14% | $106 | $111 | $117 |

### Where the two methods disagree

| Case | FY2028 EPS | FY2029 EPS | NTM EPS in Sept 2027 | P/E | Value | Rounded | Probability | DCF value in 12 months |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | $13.41 | $16.32 | $14.86 | 25 | $371.6 | $370 | 25% | $221 |
| Base | $11.77 | $12.91 | $12.34 | 21 | $259.2 | $260 | 50% | $151 |
| Bear | $8.66 | $5.29 | $6.97 | 18 | $125.5 | $125 | 25% | $47 |

The bull case adds faster growth (Data Center +45% then +22%) and a gross margin held near 74%. The bear case repeats FY2023 a year later. Growth slows to 5% in FY2028 and gross margin falls to 70%. In FY2029 Data Center revenue falls 25% and gross margin drops another 8 points to 62%, as it did from FY2022 to FY2023, which cuts operating income by 40%. For the bull and bear DCF values I fade growth from 14% and from 0% respectively.

The DCF is lower in every case. Weighted by the same probabilities it gives $142.50 in 12 months, against $253.75 from the multiples. I set the target from the multiples, because a 12-month price depends mainly on what buyers pay for the next year's earnings. The DCF does not say the shares are worth $136. At a 12% required return, it says the multiples paid for NVIDIA and its peers need more years of growth than my fade allows.

The gap still shapes the recommendation in three ways. It is one reason the bull case gets no more than 25%, since a buyer paying 25 times in 2027 would need growth no filing yet supports. It sets a selling rule: at $370 the price would need even faster growth after FY2029, so I would trim there unless new evidence has raised the case values. And it means the bear value of $125 could be too high, since the multiple itself could fall toward the DCF if growth slows.

## 8. Catalysts

A catalyst is a dated event that should show whether the thesis is right. Vera Rubin, the next data center platform, began production shipments in the October 2026 quarter, so its effect runs through every NVIDIA report below.

| Date | Event | What to look for |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-30 | Micron reports (stored earnings date) | Memory prices, which NVIDIA's 10-Q cites as a pressure on PC demand and a component of its costs |
| 2026-10-01 | NVIDIA pays its $0.25 quarterly dividend | The rate was raised from $0.01 in May 2026 |
| 2026-11-03 | AMD reports (stored earnings date) | Results of a large listed peer |
| 2026-11-17 | NVIDIA reports the October 2026 quarter | Both entry tests: January-quarter guidance and DSO. Also revenue against $105.8B to $110.2B and gross margin against 73.5% to 74.5% |
| 2026-12-09 | Broadcom reports (stored earnings date) | Results of the largest US-listed peer by market value |
| Late February 2027 | FY2027 results and annual report (last year's 10-K was filed 2026-02-25) | Second-half operating cash flow, the test for full size; supply commitments; customer concentration for the full year |
| Late May 2027 | April 2027 quarter results | First quarter of FY2028: the test of my +32% Data Center assumption |
| Late August 2027 | July 2027 quarter results (last year's were filed 2026-08-26) | Half of FY2028 reported, near the end of my 12-month horizon |
| FY2029 (from February 2028) | NVIDIA's guarantees on the SB Energy data center campus leased to OpenAI begin to take effect | Guarantees of up to $105B as each of nine data centers enters service |
| No date | Definitive agreements for the $500B-plus financing platforms announced in August 2026 | Whether the memorandums of understanding become contracts |

## 9. Risks and pre-mortem

**Customer financing.** Beyond the $99 billion of equity investments, NVIDIA had committed $25 billion more at 26 July 2026. Its cloud service commitments typically run six years, and the OpenAI guarantee covers lease and power payments. The 10-Q says AI clouds and model makers "lack the ability to secure long-term infrastructure contracts and investment-grade financing". Investment grade describes a borrower whose credit rating marks it as likely to repay.

**Working capital.** Working capital is the money tied up in receivables and inventory, net of what the company owes its suppliers. Receivables rose 64% in six months to $63.1 billion while quarterly revenue rose 41%. Management attributes this to extended payment terms on large multi-quarter agreements with investment-grade customers. Inventory rose 48% to $31.6 billion.

**Supply commitments.** They rose from $119 billion to $279 billion in one quarter. An inventory write-down is a charge for goods that can no longer be sold at cost. In a slowdown some commitments would become write-downs, as in FY2023 and with the H20 charge.

**Export rules and China.** The US has licensed some H200 sales to China, but China's government restricted them, and NVIDIA took a $0.4 billion charge this year. Guidance assumes no data center compute revenue from China.

**Competition.** Customers with in-house expertise can develop their own chips (10-K). I have no data on how much of their spending already goes to them.

**Pre-mortem.** A pre-mortem imagines that a call has already failed and asks why. It is September 2027 and Avoid was the wrong call. The most likely reason is that my entry tests were too strict. January guidance cleared $125 billion but DSO stayed near 60 days, because the large agreements pay late by design. My rule kept the portfolio out while Rubin shipped in volume and the shares reached my bull case. I accept that cost, because DSO is the only early check on customer financing. The second reason runs the other way. The tests passed, I bought 3.7% in November, and AI clouds and model makers could not raise enough money in 2027. The half size limits that loss to about 1.7% of the portfolio, and the exit rules below should end it sooner.

## 10. Monitoring and exit rules

A monitoring plan lists what I check each quarter and the threshold that changes my recommendation. Each figure comes from NVIDIA's own filings.

| What I check | Latest | My base case | Threshold | Action | Next reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Guidance for the next quarter | $108.0B for October | $118.8B for January | $125B or more, with DSO at or below 55 days | Initiate at 3.7% | 2026-11-17 |
| Guidance for the next quarter | $108.0B for October | $118.8B for January | Below $108.0B, a sequential fall | Stay out; cut the case values. If owned, Exit | 2026-11-17 |
| Revenue against guidance | $96.2B for July | $108.0B for October | Below $105.8B, the bottom of the range | Stay out. If owned, Exit | 2026-11-17 |
| Gross margin | 75.0% | 74.0% for October | Below 73.5%, the bottom of the range | Cut FY2028 EPS. If owned, Trim to half | Each report |
| DSO | 60 days | Not modelled | Above 70 days at the FY2027 year end | Stay out. If owned, Exit | Late February 2027 |
| Second-half cash from operations / non-GAAP net income | 75% (first half) | 80%, or $99.4B of $124.2B | 80% or more | If owned at half size, Add to 7.4% | Late February 2027 |
| The same | 75% (first half) | 80% | Below 70%, or $86.9B | Stay out. If owned, Exit | Late February 2027 |
| Data Center sequential growth in FY2028 | +18.3% (July quarter) | 4.4% a quarter; $116.1B in the April 2027 quarter | A sequential fall in any quarter | If owned, Trim to half and rewrite the cases | Late May 2027 onwards |
| Supply commitments | $279B | Not modelled | Falling while revenue guidance also falls | Stay out. If owned, Exit | Each report |
| Share price | $228.87 | $260 in 12 months | $370, the bull value | If owned, Trim to half unless a new memo has raised the case values | Daily |

**Exit rules.** An exit rule is a condition, stated before buying, under which I would sell or cut a holding. If the portfolio owns NVIDIA, these apply without a new argument:

1. Exit on any of the five Exit thresholds in the table.
2. Trim to half if gross margin falls below 73.5% or Data Center revenue falls from one quarter to the next.
3. Trim to half at $370. Exit when the expected total return from the current price, on the latest case values, falls below the 12% required return.
4. A fall in the price alone starts a review of the case values. It is never by itself a reason to sell or to buy more.

**The falsifier.** A falsifier is a specific, dated observation that would show a view is wrong. Mine is January-quarter guidance of $125 billion or more with DSO at or below 55 days, both reported on 17 November 2026. If both happen, Avoid was wrong and I recommend Initiate. If guidance clears $125 billion and DSO does not, I keep Avoid and say why in an update.

The strongest case against Avoid is that NVIDIA grows faster than any peer except Micron, at a lower multiple than most. On that reading the cash gap is only the timing of large contracts. I accept most of it, which is why the expected return is positive and the entry tests can be met within eight weeks. None of the bear thresholds would make me recommend a Short on its own; a Short would need its own memo.

## 11. What I don't know

- **Consensus.** No analyst forecasts are stored and I have no paid source.
- **Orders and pricing.** The filings I hold give no orders taken but not yet shipped, no units shipped and no prices for each unit sold. My revenue forecast rests on guidance, commitments and my own growth assumptions.
- **Customers.** I cannot see which customers owe the $63.1 billion of receivables, or how much of the $99 billion of equity investments is in customers.
- **Beyond FY2029.** No filing covers it, and the DCF depends on it more than on anything else.
- **The probabilities.** The 25/50/25 weights, and the move to 35/50/15 after a strong November report, are my judgment. The recommendation turns on them as much as on the model.
- **The required return.** It rests on a 13-week Treasury bill in place of a 10-year yield, a noisy one-year beta and a premium I chose. A beta of 1.46 would close the 0.7-point gap.
- **The rest of the portfolio.** The size above applies the portfolio's rule to NVIDIA alone. Its correlation with other holdings is the PM's check.
- **Revenue check.** An automatic check compares the stored 12-month revenue ($303.0 billion) with the last fiscal year ($215.9 billion) and calls the 40% gap an error. The stored figure is right: the last four quarters sum to exactly $302,969 million.
- **History.** Filed EPS before FY2023 is on older share bases (restated by factors of 40 and 10). The stored history has no capital expenditure. Free cash flow over the past 12 months ($127.0 billion) is the stored figure, which with the filings implies $7.4 billion of capital expenditure over the past year.
- **Cash.** The stored cash and investments figure is $71.6 billion; the 10-Q gives $56.6 billion of cash and debt securities. I use the filing for NVIDIA's key data. The peer table uses stored figures for every company, which gives NVIDIA 27.2 times EBITDA instead of 27.3.
- **Peers.** Intel's stored EBITDA ($123 million) is wrong according to the archive's sector guide, so its EV/EBITDA is excluded. Marvell has no stored EBITDA. Taiwan Semiconductor has no stored 12-month figures and Arm is not stored, so both are left out. Peers' latest quarters end between May and August 2026.
- **Dates.** The next earnings date (2026-11-17) is a stored field; the company has not announced it. Later dates are estimates from last year's filing dates. I have not confirmed whether FY2027 has 52 or 53 weeks.
- **Sources with limits.** The sector guide warns that its prose has not been checked against the data. The stored 10-K business section stops before its competition section, and the stored risk factors stop at 42,000 characters.

## Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| 10-K | The annual report a US company files with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). |
| 10-Q | The quarterly report a US company files with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). |
| 52-week range | The lowest and highest closing prices of the past year. |
| Accounts receivable | Money customers owe for goods already delivered. |
| Action | The step a memo asks the portfolio manager to take: Initiate, Add, Hold, Trim, Exit, Avoid or Short. |
| Add | Buying more of a stock the portfolio already owns. |
| Average daily volume | The number of shares traded on an average day, here over the past three months. |
| Avoid | Owning none of a stock. |
| Base case | The middle outcome the analyst thinks plausible, built from stated assumptions. |
| Basis point | One hundredth of a percentage point. |
| Bear case | The bad outcome the analyst thinks plausible, built from stated assumptions. |
| Beta | How much a stock tends to move for each 1% move in the market. |
| Blume adjustment | Moving a measured beta one third of the way toward 1.0, because betas tend to drift there. |
| Bull case | The good outcome the analyst thinks plausible, built from stated assumptions. |
| Buyback | The company buying its own shares, which reduces the share count. |
| Capital asset pricing model (CAPM) | A formula that sets the required return at the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium. |
| Capital expenditure (capex) | Spending on equipment and buildings. |
| Cash conversion | The share of profit that arrives as cash from operations. |
| Catalyst | A dated event that should show whether the thesis is right. |
| Comparable companies (comps) | Listed businesses similar enough that their valuation ratios give a reference point. |
| Consensus estimates | The average of other analysts' forecasts. |
| Cost of equity | The required return for shareholders. |
| Cost of revenue | The cost of the goods or services a company sold. |
| Cyclical | Describes a business whose profits rise and fall with its industry's spending rather than growing steadily. |
| Days sales outstanding (DSO) | Receivables divided by a quarter's revenue, times 91 days. |
| Diluted shares | The share count including options and awards that would become shares. |
| Discount rate | The annual return an investor requires for the risk, used to reduce future cash to today's money. |
| Discounted cash flow (DCF) | A model that values a company as the sum of its future free cash flows, each reduced to today's money. |
| Dividend | Cash paid to shareholders for each share. |
| Dividend yield | A year's dividends as a share of the price. |
| Earnings per share (EPS) | The profit attributable to each share. |
| Earnings release (Form 8-K) | The press release, filed with the SEC on Form 8-K, in which a company announces its quarterly results. |
| EBITDA | Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. |
| Enterprise value (EV) | Market capitalisation plus debt minus cash, roughly the price of the whole business free of its financing. |
| Equity risk premium | The extra annual return required for owning shares instead of government debt. |
| Estimate (E) | A forecast figure, marked E after the year, as in FY2027E. |
| EV/EBITDA | Enterprise value divided by EBITDA. |
| EV/revenue | Enterprise value divided by revenue, useful when earnings are small or negative. |
| Exit | Selling all of a holding. |
| Exit rule | A condition, stated before buying, under which the analyst would sell or cut a holding. |
| Expected return | The percentage gain from the last close to the probability-weighted value, plus any dividends expected over the same 12 months. |
| Fabless | Designing chips but paying outside foundries and contract manufacturers to make them. |
| Falsifier | A specific, dated observation that would show a view is wrong. |
| FCF yield | Free cash flow divided by market capitalisation. |
| Fiscal year (FY) | The twelve months a company's accounts cover. |
| Forward P/E | Price divided by forecast earnings per share. |
| Free cash flow (FCF) | The cash left after running the business and paying for equipment. |
| Free cash flow margin | Free cash flow as a share of revenue. |
| GAAP | The US accounting rules that a company's reported results follow. |
| Graphics processing unit (GPU) | A processor that runs many calculations in parallel. |
| Gross margin | Revenue minus the cost of revenue, as a share of revenue. |
| Guidance | Management's own published forecast. |
| Hold | Keeping a holding at its current size. |
| Inference | Running a trained artificial intelligence model to produce answers. |
| Initiate | Buying a first holding in a stock. |
| Inventory write-down | A charge for goods that can no longer be sold at cost. |
| Investment grade | A credit rating that marks a borrower as likely to repay. |
| Investment memo | The note in which an analyst asks the portfolio manager to act. |
| Investment thesis | The short argument for why a stock is mispriced, or why it is not. |
| Management's discussion and analysis (MD&A) | The section of a 10-Q or 10-K where management explains the results. |
| Market capitalisation | The share price times the number of shares, the market value of all the equity. |
| Mid-year convention | Treating each year's cash as arriving in the middle of that year. |
| Monitoring plan | The figures the analyst checks each quarter, with the threshold that would change the recommendation. |
| n/a | Not available. |
| n/m | Not meaningful, as for a P/E when earnings are negative. |
| Net cash | Cash minus debt. |
| Net debt | Debt minus cash. |
| Net margin | Net income as a share of revenue. |
| Next twelve months (NTM) | The four quarters following a given date. |
| Non-GAAP | The company's adjusted version of its results, which leaves out items it considers unusual. |
| Operating expenses | The costs of running the business beyond making the product, such as research, selling and administration. |
| Operating income | The profit left after the cost of revenue and operating expenses. |
| Operating margin | Operating income as a share of revenue. |
| Other income | Income from outside operations, such as interest and gains or losses on investments. |
| P/E | Price divided by earnings per share. |
| Percentage point | The unit of difference between two percentages. |
| Portfolio manager (PM) | The person who decides what the portfolio owns and in what size. |
| Position size | A holding's value as a share of the portfolio's value. |
| Pre-mortem | Imagining that a call has already failed and asking why. |
| Price target | The analyst's estimate of what the shares will be worth in 12 months. |
| Priced in | The growth and margins that today's price needs in order to be a fair price. |
| Probability-weighted value | Each case's value multiplied by its probability, with the results added. |
| Required return | The annual return a stock must offer to pay for its risk. |
| Revenue concentration | The share of sales that comes from a few buyers. |
| Reverse DCF | Working backwards from the price to the growth it requires. |
| Risk budget | A holding's size times its volatility. |
| Risk-free rate | The return on US government debt. |
| Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) | The US agency that regulates public companies and receives their filings. |
| Segment | A part of the business for which the company reports revenue and profit separately. |
| Sensitivity table | A table showing how a result changes when two assumptions change together. |
| Sequential growth | Growth over the previous quarter. |
| Short | Selling borrowed shares, a trade that profits if the price falls. |
| Stock split | Giving each shareholder more shares, each worth proportionately less, with no change in the company's value. |
| Stock-based compensation | The cost of paying employees in shares. |
| Supply commitments | Contracts to buy parts and manufacturing capacity in the future. |
| Terminal value | A figure standing in for every year after the forecast, assuming cash flow grows at a constant rate forever. |
| Total return | The change in price plus dividends received, as a share of the starting price. |
| Training | Building an artificial intelligence model from data. |
| Trim | Selling part of a holding. |
| Unrealised gain | An increase in the value of a holding that has not been sold. |
| Valuation multiple | A price divided by a measure of profit or size. |
| Variant perception | Where the analyst's forecast differs from what the price requires, with a checkable reason the price has not yet moved. |
| Volatility | How widely a stock's daily price changes vary, stated as a yearly figure. |
| Weighted average cost of capital (WACC) | The cost of debt and the cost of equity blended by their weights in the company's capital. |
| Working capital | Money tied up in receivables and inventory, net of what the company owes its suppliers. |
